concepts.name: Scarcity of Labelled Data
concepts.summary: The problem the paper starts from: raw text is abundant, but human-annotated data for any one task is small and expensive.
concepts.explanation:
Deep models for language tasks are normally fitted on manually annotated examples. Producing those annotations costs people, time and money, so the datasets stay small relative to what a large model could absorb.

Raw text costs nothing by comparison. It exists in enormous quantity and needs no annotator at all.

The abstract states the gap plainly: large unlabeled corpora are plentiful while labelled data for specific tasks is scarce, which makes it hard for discriminatively trained models to perform adequately.

The paper's whole design follows from trying to spend the abundant resource to relieve the scarce one. It adds a second motivation as well: even where supervision is plentiful, learning representations without labels can still give a boost.

concepts.name: Generative vs Discriminative Training
concepts.summary: Two ways of framing what a model predicts: the data itself, or a label given the data.
concepts.explanation:
A generative objective asks the model to put probability on the data. For text that means predicting the next token from the tokens before it, which needs no labels.

A discriminative objective asks for $P(y \mid x)$: a label given an input. Every training step then consumes one annotated example.

The paper's title stacks the two in order — [[generative-pretraining|generative pre-training]], then discriminative fine-tuning. That ordering is what lets it spend unlabelled text first and small labelled sets second.

When the paper says prior systems were discriminatively trained, it means the second kind of signal was all they had.

concepts.name: Natural Language Understanding
concepts.summary: The umbrella label the paper uses for a set of diverse supervised text tasks, each with its own dataset and its own notion of a correct answer.
concepts.explanation:
The paper opens by saying natural language understanding is not one task but a collection of them. It names textual entailment, question answering, [[semantic-similarity]] assessment and document classification.

Each comes with its own labelled dataset, its own input format and its own scoring metric.

That diversity is what makes the central claim interesting: one model, pre-trained once, is asked to handle all of them. In the experiments the collection is twelve datasets grouped into four task types.

Treating them as one family is a framing choice rather than a fact about language. The paper earns it by showing a single set of pre-trained weights transfers across the group.

concepts.name: Semi-Supervised Learning for NLP
concepts.summary: The family of methods that combine a large unlabelled corpus with a small labelled dataset, which the paper places itself inside.
concepts.explanation:
Semi-supervised learning uses both labelled and unlabelled data for the same end task. The related-work section says this is the category the paper broadly falls under.

It then sorts prior work into a rough chronology. The earliest methods computed word- and phrase-level statistics from unlabelled text and fed them into a supervised model as extra features.

Later work replaced those hand-built counts with learned word embeddings, and more recent work moved beyond single words to phrase and sentence representations.

The paper's own contribution sits at the far end of that progression. It transfers an entire pre-trained network rather than a table of vectors or a fixed feature channel.

concepts.name: Pre-Trained Word Embedding Transfer
concepts.summary: Training one vector per word on unlabelled text, then reusing that table inside a supervised model for a different task.
concepts.explanation:
A word embedding table is fitted on a large corpus with a co-occurrence-style objective and no task labels. The resulting vectors are then dropped into a supervised model as its input layer.

The introduction calls this the most compelling evidence so far that unsupervised learning helps, pointing at a range of tasks it has improved.

The paper's criticism is narrow and specific. This transfers word-level information only: one vector per word type says nothing about how that word behaves in a particular sentence, and nothing about phrase or sentence meaning.

The paper says it aims instead at higher-level semantics, which is why it transfers a whole network rather than a lookup table.

citedFrom.refText: T. Mikolov et al. Distributed representations of words and phrases and their compositionality. NIPS, 2013. / J. Pennington, R. Socher, and C. Manning. Glove: Global vectors for word representation. EMNLP, 2014.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The objectives that produce these vectors live in those papers; this one cites them as prior evidence.

concepts.name: Phrase- and Sentence-Level Embeddings
concepts.summary: Methods that learn one vector for a whole phrase or sentence from unlabelled text, then use it as a feature for the target task.
concepts.explanation:
These methods answer the word-level limitation by encoding a longer span into a single fixed vector. The encoder is trained on unlabelled text with some self-supervised signal, then frozen and used as a feature extractor.

The related-work section cites a cluster of such approaches, including skip-thought vectors and paragraph-level representations, as the closest predecessors in spirit.

The difference is where the representation stops. A sentence vector is a bottleneck: everything the target task can use must survive compression into that one vector.

This paper instead keeps a hidden state per position and continues training the encoder itself on the target task.

concepts.name: Unsupervised Pre-Training as a Category
concepts.summary: The branch of semi-supervised learning where unlabelled data chooses a starting point for the weights instead of changing the supervised objective.
concepts.explanation:
The related-work section draws a line here. In some semi-supervised methods the unlabelled data enters through an extra term in the loss during supervised training.

In unsupervised pre-training it enters earlier and differently. It is used to find a good initialization, and supervised training then proceeds normally from those weights.

The paper's own wording is that the goal is to find a good initialization point instead of modifying the supervised learning objective. This is the category it places its two-stage recipe in.

The technique predates its use in NLP: the section traces it to layer-by-layer training of deep networks on image classification and regression.

concepts.name: Pre-Training as a Regularization Scheme
concepts.summary: The cited finding that pre-training helps not only by easing optimization but by landing the network somewhere that generalizes better.
concepts.explanation:
One reading of pre-training is that it just gives supervised optimization an easier start. A later study argued for a different reading.

It found that pre-training acts as a regularization scheme, enabling better generalization in deep networks. On that account the unlabelled data constrains where supervised training may begin, and the constraint itself limits overfitting on a small labelled set.

The paper cites this framing directly and does not re-derive it.

It matters for the story here because several of the twelve target datasets are small, so an initialization that generalizes is worth more than one that merely converges fast.

citedFrom.refText: D. Erhan, Y. Bengio, A. Courville, P.-A. Manzagol, P. Vincent, and S. Bengio. Why does unsupervised pre-training help deep learning? JMLR, 2010.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The regularization claim is an empirical result established there and asserted here in one sentence.

concepts.name: Auxiliary Training Objectives
concepts.summary: The other branch: add a second unsupervised loss term alongside the supervised loss, so the model keeps learning from raw text while it learns the task.
concepts.explanation:
Instead of using unlabelled data first and then setting it aside, the extra objective runs at the same time as supervised training. The total loss becomes a sum of the task loss and the auxiliary loss.

The related-work section presents this as a separate line with its own history, going back to training one shared network on several NLP tasks at once.

The paper's position is slightly two-sided. Its own fine-tuning does use an auxiliary objective.

But it also reports that pre-training already learns several linguistic aspects relevant to the target tasks, which implies the auxiliary term is doing less work here than it did for methods with no pre-training.

concepts.name: Feature-Based Transfer
concepts.summary: The competing transfer style: freeze a pre-trained language or translation model and feed its hidden states into a separate task model as extra input features.
concepts.explanation:
Here the pre-trained network is a fixed producer of vectors. A new task-specific model is built on top and trained from scratch on the labelled data, taking those vectors as additional inputs alongside ordinary word embeddings.

The related-work section describes it as using hidden representations from a pre-trained language or machine translation model as auxiliary features while training a supervised model on the target task.

The paper's objection is about cost. Each target task needs its own new model, so the approach involves a substantial amount of new parameters per task.

The comparison as stated is about parameter cost and architectural effort. The accuracy comparison is left to the experiments.

concepts.name: Deep Contextualized Word Representations (ELMo)
concepts.summary: The best-known feature-based approach: hidden states from a pre-trained bidirectional language model, added as features to a task model.
concepts.explanation:
A language model is trained on unlabelled text and then frozen. Its internal states give each token a vector that depends on the surrounding sentence, unlike a static word embedding.

Those vectors feed a task-specific network that is trained separately.

The paper cites this line repeatedly. It is the feature-based contrast to fine-tuning, the source of the 1B Word Benchmark corpus comparison, and the contextual features inside the BiLSTM + ELMo + Attn baselines the results tables measure against.

The difference from this paper's setup is that the pre-trained weights are never updated by the task.

citedFrom.refText: M. E. Peters, M. Neumann, M. Iyyer, M. Gardner, C. Clark, K. Lee, and L. Zettlemoyer. Deep contextualized word representations. NAACL, 2018.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The bidirectional language model and the layer-mixing scheme that produce the features are defined there; this paper summarizes it in a clause.

concepts.name: Per-Task Parameter Cost
concepts.summary: The quantity the paper uses to separate its approach from feature-based transfer: how many freshly initialized parameters each new task needs.
concepts.explanation:
Every parameter that is new for a task must be fitted from that task's labelled data, which is the scarce resource.

[[feature-based-transfer|Feature-based transfer]] needs a whole task model on top of the frozen encoder, so the count is large.

Fine-tuning starts every parameter from a pre-trained value and adds only a thin task-specific layer, so the count is small.

The related-work section frames the difference exactly this way, contrasting a substantial amount of new parameters for each separate target task with minimal changes to the model architecture during transfer. It states the contrast qualitatively and gives no parameter counts.

concepts.name: Language-Model Pre-Training Then Fine-Tuning
concepts.summary: The line of work the paper calls closest to its own: pre-train with a language modelling objective, then fine-tune the whole network on a supervised task.
concepts.explanation:
The related-work section identifies two prior systems with exactly this shape, both applied to [[text-classification]].

The paper accepts the shape and changes two things. The first is the network: those systems used LSTMs, while this one uses a transformer, which the paper argues captures longer-range structure.

The second is the range of tasks. This paper adds [[natural-language-inference]], paraphrase detection and story completion to classification.

So the claimed contribution is not the recipe but what it is built from and how far it stretches.

concepts.name: Semi-Supervised Sequence Learning
concepts.summary: Earlier work that pre-trained a recurrent network with a language modelling or autoencoding objective and fine-tuned it for text classification.
concepts.explanation:
This is one of the two systems the related-work section names as closest in method.

It established that a recurrent sequence model pre-trained on unlabelled text could be fine-tuned to improve classification accuracy.

The paper's stated difference is the model class and the breadth of tasks, not the training procedure. It is cited in a single sentence, so the objective and schedule are not reproduced here.

citedFrom.refText: A. M. Dai and Q. V. Le. Semi-supervised sequence learning. NIPS, 2015.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The pre-training objectives and fine-tuning procedure are defined there; this paper names the result only.

concepts.name: Universal Language Model Fine-Tuning
concepts.summary: A contemporaneous method that fine-tunes a pre-trained LSTM language model for text classification using a carefully staged schedule.
concepts.explanation:
This system shares the paper's two-stage shape but puts considerable design effort into how fine-tuning is run.

The introduction refers to that kind of effort as intricate learning schemes, and lists it among the open questions about how best to transfer representations.

The related-work section then names the same work as one of the two closest predecessors. The contrast drawn is again the LSTM backbone and the restriction to [[text-classification]].

citedFrom.refText: J. Howard and S. Ruder. Universal language model fine-tuning for text classification. ACL, 2018.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The staged fine-tuning schedule this paper calls intricate is specified there, not here.

concepts.name: Short-Range Limitation of LSTM Pre-Training
concepts.summary: The paper's argument that recurrent pre-trained models keep their predictions local, capping how much structure they transfer.
concepts.explanation:
The related-work section says that although pre-training helps those systems capture some linguistic information, their use of LSTMs restricts prediction ability to a short range.

The reasoning is about how information travels in a recurrent network. Everything from the past has to pass through a single state vector, one step at a time.

The paper contrasts this with attention, which reaches any earlier position directly, and says its choice allows longer-range linguistic structure to be captured.

The support offered is an architectural argument plus downstream results, not a direct measurement of dependency length.

concepts.name: Which Pre-Training Objective to Use
concepts.summary: The first open question the introduction identifies: nobody knows which unsupervised objective yields text representations that transfer best.
concepts.explanation:
Several objectives had been tried for learning transferable representations. The introduction lists language modelling, machine translation and discourse coherence.

Its observation is that none dominates: each method outperforms the others on different tasks, with a footnote pointing at the GLUE leaderboard as evidence.

That is a stated uncertainty rather than a rhetorical setup.

The paper resolves it by picking language modelling and showing results, not by arguing the choice through in advance.

concepts.name: How to Transfer Learned Representations
concepts.summary: The second open question: given a pre-trained representation, there was no consensus on how best to move it into a target task.
concepts.explanation:
The introduction lists three transfer techniques then in use. One makes task-specific changes to the model architecture. Another uses intricate learning schemes during fine-tuning. A third adds auxiliary learning objectives to the supervised loss.

The paper's summary is that these uncertainties, together with the objective question, had made it difficult to develop effective semi-supervised approaches for language processing.

Its own answer is to change the input rather than the architecture, keeping the transfer machinery simple.

concepts.name: Two-Stage Training Procedure
concepts.summary: The paper's recipe: learn the network's initial parameters with a language modelling objective on unlabelled text, then adapt those same parameters to each target task with its supervised objective.
concepts.explanation:
Stage one trains a high-capacity language model on a large corpus of plain text. No labels are involved, and the product the paper cares about is a set of weights rather than any prediction.

Stage two takes those weights as the starting point and continues training on a labelled dataset using that task's loss.

Both stages train the same model. The second begins from the first's parameters rather than from scratch, which is what makes this transfer rather than feature extraction.

The architecture stays essentially fixed across the two stages and across target tasks. That is what lets one pre-trained model serve twelve evaluations with only a small per-task addition.

The paper states the goal as learning a universal representation that transfers with little adaptation, and adds an assumption that keeps the recipe cheap: the target tasks need not come from the same domain as the unlabelled corpus.

concepts.name: Transfer Learning Here
concepts.summary: Reusing parameters learned on one task as the starting point for another. Here the pre-trained language model's weights initialize every target task.
concepts.explanation:
In this setup everything below the classifier is transferred: the embeddings and all twelve transformer blocks start from their pre-trained values.

Section 3.3 uses the term to make a criticism. If a method adds new task-specific architecture on top of transferred representations, those new components start from random weights and get no benefit from transfer.

Section 5 measures what the transfer buys. Removing pre-training entirely and training the same transformer directly on the supervised tasks costs 14.8%.

concepts.name: No Domain Match Required
concepts.summary: The stated assumption that the unlabelled pre-training corpus need not come from the same domain as the target tasks.
concepts.explanation:
Some transfer setups require the source data to resemble the destination data. The introduction says plainly that this one does not.

That is what makes a single pre-training run reusable across twelve datasets of different kinds.

It also means the pre-training corpus can be chosen for its own properties, such as long contiguous passages, rather than to match any particular benchmark.

concepts.name: Generative Pre-Training (Stage One)
concepts.summary: Train a multi-layer transformer decoder to predict each next token on a large unlabelled corpus, and keep the weights rather than the outputs.
concepts.explanation:
The paper is handed a corpus of tokens $U = \{u_1,\dots,u_n\}$ with no labels attached. Training maximizes the likelihood the model assigns to each token given the tokens before it.

Nothing about the target tasks enters at this stage. The only thing being fit is the text.

The paper calls this generative because the objective models the data itself rather than a label conditioned on the data. Every position in the corpus supplies a training signal for free.

Capacity matters here, because stage two only pays off if stage one stored something worth transferring. The concrete model is twelve layers of 768-dimensional states, trained for 100 epochs.

The objective itself is described as standard. What the paper claims is the scale of the corpus and the choice of architecture.

The conclusion adds a claim about what the model picks up along the way: [[world-knowledge]], and an ability to process long-range dependencies.

concepts.name: Language Modelling Objective $L_1$
concepts.summary: The pre-training loss $L_1(U)=\sum_i \log P(u_i \mid u_{i-k},\dots,u_{i-1};\Theta)$: maximize the log-probability the model gives each token given the tokens before it.
concepts.explanation:
Take a position $i$ in the corpus. The model reads the $k$ tokens before it and produces a distribution over the vocabulary for position $i$.

The objective picks out the log-probability that distribution assigned to the token that actually appeared.

Those log-probabilities are summed over every position in the corpus, and the sum is maximized by stochastic gradient descent over the parameters $\Theta$.

Only preceding tokens condition each prediction. The objective is strictly left-to-right, which is what makes [[masked-self-attention|masked self-attention]] necessary in the architecture.

Because no annotation is needed to build an example, every token of the corpus is a training case.

The paper labels this term $L_1$ and reuses the label in Section 3.2, where it returns as an auxiliary term during fine-tuning.

concepts.name: Maximum-Likelihood Training
concepts.summary: Fitting parameters by maximizing the log-probability the model assigns to the observed data. Assumed known.
concepts.explanation:
Both $L_1$ and $L_2$ in this paper are written as sums of log-probabilities to be maximized, which in practice is minimizing cross-entropy by gradient descent.

The paper assumes this and does not comment further.

concepts.name: World Knowledge from Pre-Training
concepts.summary: The conclusion's claim that predicting text over a large corpus leaves the model with facts and expectations about the world.
concepts.explanation:
The conclusion states that the model acquires significant world knowledge during pre-training, and that this knowledge transfers to the discriminative tasks.

The implied mechanism is indirect. To predict text well a model has to encode regularities about what tends to be true and what tends to happen next.

The Story Cloze result is the strongest supporting number, since choosing a story ending rewards exactly that kind of expectation.

The claim is made at summary level. The paper does not isolate world knowledge from other things pre-training might supply.

concepts.name: Multi-Layer Transformer Decoder
concepts.summary: The language model is a stack of transformer blocks used as a decoder only: masked multi-head self-attention over the context, then position-wise feedforward layers.
concepts.explanation:
The paper takes the transformer and keeps only the decoder side of it, following the variant used for generating Wikipedia from long input sequences.

Each layer applies multi-headed self-attention over the input context tokens, then a position-wise feedforward network. Stacking gives $h_l = \mathrm{transformer\_block}(h_{l-1})$ for $l \in [1,n]$, with $n = 12$ in the trained model.

Layer zero is the token embeddings plus the position embeddings. The top layer's states are projected back to the vocabulary to give the output distribution.

The paper's argument for this stack over a recurrent one is that its attentional memory handles long-range dependencies better.

Section 5 puts a number on that argument. Swapping in a single-layer 2048-unit LSTM under the same framework costs 5.6 average score.

citedFrom.refText: P. J. Liu, M. Saleh, E. Pot, B. Goodrich, R. Sepassi, L. Kaiser, and N. Shazeer. Generating wikipedia by summarizing long sequences. ICLR, 2018.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The decoder-only transformer variant the paper adopts is defined there; the paper cites it in place of describing the variant.

concepts.name: Transformer Architecture
concepts.summary: The stacked self-attention and feed-forward architecture this paper builds on. Assumed known.
concepts.explanation:
A stack of identical blocks, each combining multi-head self-attention over all positions with a position-wise feed-forward network, plus residual connections and layer normalization.

The paper adopts it rather than introducing it, citing its results on machine translation, document generation and syntactic parsing.

What this paper changes — a [[decoder-only-stack|decoder-only stack]], [[masked-self-attention|masked self-attention]], [[learned-position-embeddings]] — is covered separately.

citedFrom.refText: A. Vaswani, N. Shazeer, N. Parmar, J. Uszkoreit, L. Jones, A. N. Gomez, Ł. Kaiser, and I. Polosukhin. Attention is all you need. NIPS, 2017.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The architecture is defined there and adopted wholesale here.

concepts.name: Decoder-Only Stack
concepts.summary: The model drops the encoder half of the original encoder-decoder transformer and keeps one stack that attends only to its own past tokens.
concepts.explanation:
The original transformer has two stacks. An encoder reads a source sequence with unrestricted self-attention, so every source position sees every other.

The decoder generates a target sequence. It attends to its own previous outputs through [[masked-self-attention|masked self-attention]], and separately to the encoder's states through a cross-attention sublayer.

Language modelling has no source sequence. There is nothing to encode and nothing to cross-attend to.

So the paper keeps one stack and removes the cross-attention sublayer. Each block is left with masked self-attention followed by a feedforward network, and Section 4.1 states the result directly: a 12-layer decoder-only transformer with masked self-attention heads.

The consequence carries into stage two. Every input the model ever sees, for any task, has to arrive as a single ordered sequence read left to right — which is what the input transformations then have to arrange.

citedFrom.refText: A. Vaswani, N. Shazeer, N. Parmar, J. Uszkoreit, L. Jones, A. N. Gomez, Ł. Kaiser, and I. Polosukhin. Attention is all you need. NIPS, 2017.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The encoder-decoder design this stack is a trimmed version of, including the cross-attention sublayer that gets removed, is defined there.

concepts.name: Masked Self-Attention
concepts.summary: Self-attention restricted so each position attends only to itself and earlier positions, never to later ones.
concepts.explanation:
Plain self-attention lets every position attend to every other, including positions to its right. In a language model that would be fatal: the model would see token $u_i$ while being asked to predict $u_i$, and $L_1$ would be trivial to maximize.

The fix is a mask. Before the attention softmax, the scores for all positions to the right of the current one are driven to $-\infty$, so after normalization their weights are zero.

Each position then summarizes only $u_{i-k},\dots,u_i$, which is exactly the conditioning set written down in $L_1$.

The practical payoff is throughput. One forward pass over a 512-token sequence yields a valid next-token prediction at every position at once, rather than one prediction per pass.

All [[twelve-attention-heads]] at all twelve layers are masked this way.

The mask stays in place during fine-tuning too. That is why a classification input must be one ordered sequence, and why the label is read off the final token rather than pooled across positions.

concepts.name: Input Representation $h_0$
concepts.summary: The layer-zero input is the token embeddings of the context plus the position embeddings: $h_0 = UW_e + W_p$.
concepts.explanation:
$U = (u_{-k},\dots,u_{-1})$ is the context vector of tokens. Multiplying by the [[token-embedding-matrix]] $W_e$ replaces each token id with that token's embedding row.

Adding $W_p$ then adds a second vector that depends on which slot the token occupies, not on which token it is.

Note that this is a sum, not a concatenation. Both matrices produce vectors of the same width, 768 in this model, and they are added element-wise.

That sum is what the first transformer block reads. Position has to be injected here because self-attention on its own treats its inputs as an unordered set.

concepts.name: Token Embedding Matrix $W_e$
concepts.summary: $W_e$ maps each vocabulary token to a dense vector, and its transpose is reused at the output to score candidate next tokens.
concepts.explanation:
Each row of $W_e$ is the vector for one vocabulary entry. Context tokens are looked up in it to build the layer-zero input.

The same matrix appears again at the top of the model, as $W_e^T$, when the final hidden states are turned into a distribution over tokens.

The vocabulary is not words. It is a byte-pair encoding vocabulary built with 40,000 merges, so rows correspond to subword units.

Reusing one matrix at both ends keeps the parameter count down and ties a token's input and output representations together.

concepts.name: Learned Position Embeddings
concepts.summary: Position information comes from a trained matrix $W_p$, one vector per slot, rather than from the fixed sinusoids of the original transformer.
concepts.explanation:
Self-attention computes a weighted sum over positions, and nothing in that computation depends on order. Permute the inputs and the same vectors come back permuted.

The original transformer solves this by adding fixed sinusoidal functions of the position index. Those values are computed, not learned.

This paper instead makes $W_p$ a parameter matrix: one trainable 768-dimensional vector for each of the 512 slots in the context window, added to the token embedding at that slot and updated by the same gradients as everything else.

One consequence is that the table has a fixed height. There is no vector for position 513, so a learned scheme does not extrapolate past the trained window the way a sinusoid formally can.

The paper reports no ablation isolating this choice, so it reads as a design preference rather than a demonstrated gain.

citedFrom.refText: A. Vaswani, N. Shazeer, N. Parmar, J. Uszkoreit, L. Jones, A. N. Gomez, Ł. Kaiser, and I. Polosukhin. Attention is all you need. NIPS, 2017.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The sinusoidal scheme being replaced is defined there.

concepts.name: Output Distribution $P(u) = \mathrm{softmax}(h_n W_e^T)$
concepts.summary: The top block's states are multiplied by the transpose of the token embedding matrix and softmaxed to give a distribution over the vocabulary.
concepts.explanation:
Equation 2 ends with $P(u) = \mathrm{softmax}(h_n W_e^T)$, where $h_n$ holds the states leaving the top transformer block.

Multiplying a 768-dimensional state by $W_e^T$ gives one score per vocabulary entry. Each score is the dot product between the state and that token's embedding row, so a token scores highly when the state points the same way its embedding does.

The softmax turns those scores into a distribution.

Because the output projection is the transpose of the input embedding matrix, no separate output matrix is trained. This is the distribution $L_1$ scores during pre-training, and the same one the auxiliary objective scores again during fine-tuning.

concepts.name: Long-Range Dependencies in Text
concepts.summary: Relationships spanning many tokens, such as a pronoun and an antecedent several sentences back, or an exam question and the passage detail that answers it.
concepts.explanation:
Some of the information a model needs is nearby, and some is far away. A model that reaches back only a few tokens handles the first kind and not the second.

The paper makes the second kind load-bearing. The introduction says the transformer gives a more structured memory for handling long-term dependencies than alternatives such as recurrent networks, because attention keeps every earlier position addressable instead of compressing the past into one state vector.

The related-work section reuses the same argument against LSTM-based pre-training, and the conclusion names text with long-range dependencies as the kind of data the approach works best with.

The support offered is transfer performance across tasks rather than a dedicated probe of dependency length.

concepts.name: Supervised Fine-Tuning (Stage Two)
concepts.summary: Run labelled inputs through the pre-trained model, take the final block's activation at the last token, and train a linear layer on it to predict the label.
concepts.explanation:
The labelled dataset $C$ holds instances made of a token sequence $x_1,\dots,x_m$ and a label $y$. The whole sequence is passed through the pre-trained transformer.

The activation of the final transformer block at the last token, written $h_l^m$, is taken as the representation of the instance.

A linear layer with parameters $W_y$ maps that vector to one score per class, and a softmax turns the scores into $P(y \mid x_1,\dots,x_m)$.

Training maximizes $L_2(C)$, the summed log-probability of the correct labels, with gradients flowing back through the entire pre-trained stack. The pre-trained representations are adjusted by the task, not merely consulted by it.

The word discriminative marks the change of objective: the model now predicts a label given an input rather than predicting the input itself.

This stage is short. The paper reports a learning rate of 6.25e-5, batches of 32, and three epochs sufficient for most tasks.

concepts.name: Labelled Dataset $C$
concepts.summary: $C$ denotes a target task's labelled data: input token sequences each paired with one label.
concepts.explanation:
Each instance in $C$ is a sequence $x_1,\dots,x_m$ together with a label $y$, and the length $m$ varies from instance to instance.

None of $C$ is used during pre-training. It enters only in stage two, and each of the twelve target tasks gets its own fine-tuning run from the same pre-trained weights.

Tasks whose raw inputs are not a single sequence — a premise and a hypothesis, or a document with a question and several answers — must first be converted into one.

After that conversion every target task looks the same to the model: one sequence in, one label out.

concepts.name: Final Block Activation $h_l^m$
concepts.summary: The representation fed to the classifier is the final transformer block's output at the last input token.
concepts.explanation:
The notation $h_l^m$ in Equation 3 picks position $m$, the last token, from the final block $l$.

That position is special because attention is masked. Every other position has seen only a prefix of the input; the last position is the only one that has attended to the whole sequence.

So everything the classifier learns about an instance has to be summarized in that single vector. There is no pooling over positions.

This is also why every transformed input ends with an end token. It gives the model a dedicated final slot to summarize into, which Figure 1 labels Extract.

concepts.name: Added Linear Output Layer $W_y$
concepts.summary: The one parameter matrix added on top of the pre-trained model, mapping the final activation to label scores.
concepts.explanation:
Equation 3 is $P(y \mid x_1,\dots,x_m) = \mathrm{softmax}(h_l^m W_y)$.

$W_y$ is small. With 768-dimensional states and a handful of classes it is 768 by the number of labels, a few thousand parameters against a stack of twelve blocks.

It is initialized fresh for each target task, because the label sets differ. Everything beneath it is inherited from pre-training.

A dropout at rate 0.1 is applied to this classifier during fine-tuning.

concepts.name: Supervised Objective $L_2$
concepts.summary: $L_2(C) = \sum_{(x,y)} \log P(y \mid x_1,\dots,x_m)$: the summed log-probability of the correct labels over the labelled data.
concepts.explanation:
For each instance, take the probability the model assigned to the true label and add its logarithm to the total. Maximizing that total is ordinary classification training.

Gradients do not stop at $W_y$. They flow back through the whole pre-trained stack, so fine-tuning adjusts every transformer weight.

On its own $L_2$ would be the objective for a plain fine-tune. The paper adds a second term to it in Equation 5.

concepts.name: Auxiliary Language Modelling Objective
concepts.summary: During fine-tuning the paper keeps optimizing the language modelling loss alongside the task loss: $L_3(C) = L_2(C) + \lambda\, L_1(C)$.
concepts.explanation:
The next-token loss does not disappear when stage two begins. It is recomputed on the fine-tuning data $C$ — the same task inputs, scored simply as text — and added to the classification loss with weight $\lambda$.

The paper reports two effects from including it: better generalization of the supervised model, and faster convergence.

Both are stated as empirical findings. No mechanism is offered, and the paper notes prior work observed similar gains from adding a language modelling term to a supervised objective.

Section 5 puts a limit on the claim. Ablating the term shows it helps on the [[natural-language-inference]] tasks and on [[qqp]], while smaller datasets do not benefit.

So the reported trend is that larger fine-tuning sets gain from it and smaller ones do not.

citedFrom.refText: M. Rei. Semi-supervised multitask learning for sequence labeling. ACL, 2017.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The construction this paper adopts, and its measured effect on sequence labeling, come from there; this paper cites it in one sentence.

concepts.name: Auxiliary Objective Weight $\lambda = 0.5$
concepts.summary: $\lambda$ scales the auxiliary language modelling term against the classification term. The paper sets it to 0.5.
concepts.explanation:
In $L_3 = L_2 + \lambda L_1$, setting $\lambda = 0$ recovers plain fine-tuning. Making $\lambda$ large would push the model to care more about predicting text than about getting the label right.

Section 4.1 gives the value used throughout: $\lambda$ was set to 0.5, so the language modelling term carries half the weight of the classification term in every reported result.

The paper reports no sweep over $\lambda$, so it is best read as a chosen value rather than a tuned optimum.

This single number is what the first ablation removes: setting it to zero is what without the [[auxiliary-lm-objective]] means in Table 5.

concepts.name: Minimal Extra Fine-Tuning Parameters
concepts.summary: Adapting to a new task adds only the linear layer $W_y$ and embeddings for the delimiter tokens.
concepts.explanation:
Section 3.2 states this at the end: the only extra parameters required during fine-tuning are $W_y$ and embeddings for the delimiter tokens.

No new layers, no task-specific encoder, no attention module stacked on top.

The delimiter embeddings are new because those symbols never appeared in the pre-training corpus, so their rows start randomly initialized. Everything else is a pre-trained weight being adjusted.

The abstract, introduction and related-work section all repeat the point in different words, and it is the basis of the paper's comparison against methods that add a substantial amount of new parameters per task.

concepts.name: Task-Specific Input Transformations
concepts.summary: Structured task inputs are rewritten as one ordered token sequence, so the pre-trained model can read them without architectural change.
concepts.explanation:
Pre-training saw contiguous runs of text, one sequence at a time. Many target tasks do not arrive that way.

Entailment gives an ordered sentence pair. Question answering gives a document, a question and a set of candidate answers. [[text-classification]], by contrast, already is a single sequence and can be fine-tuned directly.

Rather than build a module per task to combine those pieces, the paper concatenates them into one sequence using special tokens. Every transformation wraps the result in randomly initialized [[start-and-end-tokens]], $\langle s\rangle$ and $\langle e\rangle$.

The architecture then stays fixed and only the input formatting varies. Figure 1 draws the four cases side by side.

The abstract presents this as the difference from previous approaches: the transformations achieve effective transfer while requiring minimal changes to the model architecture. The work of handling structure moves out of the network and into the data format.

concepts.name: Structured Inputs
concepts.summary: Task inputs made of several distinct parts — ordered sentence pairs, or document/question/answer triplets — rather than one run of text.
concepts.explanation:
Section 3.3 names two shapes. Ordered sentence pairs cover entailment and similarity. Triplets of document, question and answers cover [[question-answering-and-commonsense-reasoning]].

The difficulty is that the pre-trained model has no notion of a part. It was trained on contiguous sequences, so it has no slot for the second sentence or for candidate answer three.

The transformations exist to bridge that gap. They flatten structure into order and mark the seams with a delimiter.

concepts.name: Traversal-Style Approach
concepts.summary: The strategy of walking the parts of a structured input into one ordered sequence, instead of building an architecture that mirrors the structure.
concepts.explanation:
The paper borrows the term from earlier work on entailment with neural attention, and says its task-specific input adaptations are derived from it.

The name comes from traversing a structure in a fixed order to flatten it. Applied here, a premise-hypothesis pair or a document-question-answer triple becomes one ordered stream.

The alternative the paper rejects is learning [[task-specific-architectures|task-specific architectures]] on top of transferred representations.

The cost of traversal is that the model must recover from the format whatever structure the format only implies. The delimiter is a marker, not a described relationship.

The benefit claimed is that nothing new has to be designed or learned per task, so the transformations let the paper avoid extensive changes to the architecture across tasks.

citedFrom.refText: T. Rocktäschel, E. Grefenstette, K. M. Hermann, T. Kočiský, and P. Blunsom. Reasoning about entailment with neural attention. arXiv:1509.06664, 2015.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The paper names this as the source of the traversal-style approach it adopts without describing what that approach is.

concepts.name: Start and End Tokens $\langle s\rangle$, $\langle e\rangle$
concepts.summary: Every transformed input is bracketed by a randomly initialized start token and end token.
concepts.explanation:
Section 3.3 says all transformations include adding randomly initialized start and end tokens.

Neither symbol occurs in the pre-training corpus, so neither has a pre-trained embedding. Their rows begin random and are learned during fine-tuning, alongside the delimiter embeddings.

The two are not equally important. The start token simply opens the sequence.

The end token is the final position, and it is the one whose activation the classifier reads. Figure 1 labels that slot Extract, because it is where the model must summarize the whole input.

concepts.name: Delimiter Token ($)
concepts.summary: A special `$` symbol inserted between the parts of a transformed input to mark where one part ends and the next begins.
concepts.explanation:
When a premise and a hypothesis are concatenated, nothing in the raw text says where the boundary falls. The delimiter is placed there.

It is one more symbol with a learned embedding, added at fine-tuning time. Section 3.2 counts these delimiter embeddings, together with $W_y$, as the only extra parameters fine-tuning requires.

Every structured transformation uses it: entailment, similarity, and the document-question-answer format.

The symbol carried no meaning during pre-training. Whatever the boundary means for a given task has to be learned from that task's labelled data.

concepts.name: Entailment Input Transformation
concepts.summary: The premise and hypothesis token sequences are concatenated with a delimiter between them.
concepts.explanation:
The resulting sequence is $\langle s\rangle$, the premise tokens, `$`, the hypothesis tokens, $\langle e\rangle$.

One forward pass produces the final-block activation at $\langle e\rangle$, and $W_y$ maps that to the entailment labels.

There are no separate encoders and no cross-attention between two towers. The single masked stack reads the hypothesis tokens with the premise already sitting in their context.

Because entailment has an inherent direction — whether $p$ entails $h$ is a different question from whether $h$ entails $p$ — one fixed ordering encodes the problem faithfully.

concepts.name: Similarity Input Transformation
concepts.summary: Both sentence orderings are built and processed separately, and their two final activations are added element-wise before the linear output layer.
concepts.explanation:
A single concatenation would break the task's symmetry. The stack reads left to right under a mask, so in "A $ B" the tokens of B see A, while the tokens of A never see B.

So the paper builds two sequences, one for each ordering, each with a delimiter between the sentences.

Each is processed independently and produces its own final-block activation $h_l^m$.

The two vectors are then added element-wise. Addition commutes, so swapping which sentence was called first leaves the sum unchanged, and the representation is symmetric by construction.

That single sum is what $W_y$ reads. The cost is two forward passes per example instead of one.

concepts.name: Question Answering and Commonsense Transformation
concepts.summary: Each candidate answer is concatenated onto the document and question to form its own sequence, and the resulting scores are normalized across candidates.
concepts.explanation:
The input is a context document $z$, a question $q$, and a set of possible answers $\{a_k\}$.

For each candidate $k$ the paper forms the sequence $[z; q; \$; a_k]$: the document and question run together, then a delimiter, then that one candidate.

Each sequence is processed independently by the same model, so a four-choice question costs four forward passes.

Each pass yields one scalar score, read from the final token through the output layer. A softmax over the $k$ scores turns them into a distribution across the candidate set, and the highest-probability candidate is the prediction.

Scoring is therefore comparative. A candidate is not judged good or bad in isolation; it has to beat the others for the same question. The number of output classes is set by how many candidates the question happens to have, not by $W_y$.

concepts.name: Task-Agnostic Model
concepts.summary: A single architecture, pre-trained once, applied to every task without being redesigned for any of them.
concepts.explanation:
The abstract's central claim is comparative: the general task-agnostic model outperforms discriminatively trained models that use architectures specifically crafted for each task.

Task-agnostic here means the network's structure carries no assumptions about entailment, or multiple-choice answers, or sentence pairs. Those assumptions live in the input format and in a small output layer instead.

The introduction frames the goal as learning a universal representation that transfers with little adaptation to a wide range of tasks. Universal does two jobs in that sentence: one representation rather than one per task, and a low adaptation cost.

The evidence offered is breadth. Four task types, twelve datasets, one pre-training run, with improvement on the previous best result for nine of the twelve.

concepts.name: Task-Specific Architectures
concepts.summary: The prevailing alternative: networks designed by hand around one task's structure, often stacked on top of transferred representations.
concepts.explanation:
For each task type, researchers had built architectures matched to it — cross-sentence attention for entailment, answer-scoring modules for reading comprehension — and trained them discriminatively on that task's labelled data.

Where transferred representations were used at all, they sat at the bottom. Everything above was designed and trained per task, starting from random weights each time.

The paper's complaint has two parts. It re-introduces a significant amount of task-specific customization, and [[transfer-learning]] does no work for the added components.

The introduction also lists making task-specific changes to the architecture among the open questions that had held semi-supervised NLP back.

The counter-proposal is to move the per-task work out of the architecture and into the input format.

citedFrom.refText: M. E. Peters, M. Neumann, M. Iyyer, M. Gardner, C. Clark, K. Lee, and L. Zettlemoyer. Deep contextualized word representations. NAACL, 2018.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: This is the concrete prior approach Section 3.3 contrasts against; the contrast needs its transfer scheme and what it builds on top.

concepts.name: BooksCorpus
concepts.summary: The pre-training corpus: over 7,000 unpublished books across genres. Its selling point in this paper is long stretches of contiguous text.
concepts.explanation:
BooksCorpus is the unlabelled text the language model is trained on. It contains over 7,000 unique unpublished books spanning genres such as Adventure, Fantasy and Romance.

The property the paper cares about is not the genre mix but the shape of the text. A book arrives as a long unbroken run of sentences in their original order.

That matters because the objective asks the model to predict the next token from the tokens before it. If the preceding tokens reach back across paragraphs, the model has an incentive to condition on long-range information rather than on the last few words.

The paper calls this out as its reason for preferring BooksCorpus to a similarly sized but sentence-shuffled alternative.

It reports a token-level perplexity of 18.4 on this corpus as a sanity figure for the pre-training run, and does not tie that number to any downstream claim.

citedFrom.refText: Y. Zhu, R. Kiros, R. Zemel, R. Salakhutdinov, R. Urtasun, A. Torralba, and S. Fidler. Aligning books and movies: towards story-like visual explanations by watching movies and reading books. ICCV, 2015.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The corpus is defined and collected there; its size, genre composition and collection method are not restated here.

concepts.name: Long-Range Contiguous Text
concepts.summary: Text kept in its original order across sentences and paragraphs, so a context window can span far more than one sentence.
concepts.explanation:
Contiguous means the corpus preserves the order in which sentences were written, rather than storing sentences as independent items.

When a 512-token example is cut from such a corpus, the tokens at the end of the window depend on tokens hundreds of positions earlier: a character named in one paragraph, a fact established in another.

The paper's argument is that this dependency structure is what lets a generative model learn to condition on long-range information. If the corpus never contains such dependencies, the objective never rewards learning them.

The conclusion turns the observation into advice, naming text with long-range dependencies as the kind of data the approach works best with. The evidence is the transfer results as a whole, not a controlled comparison against a shuffled corpus.

concepts.name: 1B Word Benchmark
concepts.summary: An alternative pre-training corpus of roughly the same size as BooksCorpus, but shuffled at the sentence level. The paper names it as the corpus ELMo uses.
concepts.explanation:
This is the comparison the paper draws to justify its corpus choice. The benchmark is approximately the same size as BooksCorpus, so the contrast is not about how much text is available.

The difference is ordering. The benchmark is shuffled at a sentence level, which the paper says destroys long-range structure.

After shuffling, the sentence before the current one is an unrelated sentence from elsewhere in the collection. A model trained on it can still learn within-sentence statistics, but there is no coherent discourse reaching backwards for it to exploit.

The paper notes that ELMo, which it treats as a similar approach, trains on this corpus.

concepts.name: Token-Level Perplexity of 18.4
concepts.summary: The paper reports its language model reaching a token-level perplexity of 18.4 on BooksCorpus, offered as evidence pre-training fit the corpus.
concepts.explanation:
Perplexity summarizes how surprised a model is by the text it scores. It is the exponential of the average negative log-probability per token, so 18.4 means the model is on average about as uncertain as if choosing uniformly among 18.4 options at each token.

The qualifier token-level matters. Because the paper works in byte-pair units rather than whole words, the average is taken over subword tokens.

That makes the number not directly comparable to word-level perplexities quoted elsewhere.

The paper offers it as a single sanity figure and draws no downstream conclusion from it.

concepts.name: Model Specification
concepts.summary: The exact architecture trained: a 12-layer decoder-only transformer with 768-dimensional states, 12 attention heads and 3072-dimensional inner feed-forward states.
concepts.explanation:
This is the concrete configuration behind every number in the results. The paper says it largely follows the original transformer work, then lists where it fixes the free parameters.

The stack is 12 layers deep. Each layer carries a 768-dimensional hidden state per position, splits attention into 12 heads, and expands to 3072 dimensions inside its position-wise feed-forward sublayer.

Two choices depart from the original. The stack is decoder-only with [[masked-self-attention|masked self-attention]] rather than an encoder-decoder pair, and positions are represented by learned embeddings rather than fixed sinusoids.

Layer normalization is used extensively throughout the model, and the paper reports that a simple $\mathcal{N}(0, 0.02)$ [[weight-initialization]] was sufficient because of it.

Everything downstream — the fine-tuning results, the layer-transfer curve, the ablations — is this one model, so the spec is the fixed point the experiments vary around.

citedFrom.refText: A. Vaswani, N. Shazeer, N. Parmar, J. Uszkoreit, L. Jones, A. N. Gomez, Ł. Kaiser, and I. Polosukhin. Attention is all you need. NIPS, 2017.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The architecture the spec largely follows is defined there; this section records only the deltas and the hyperparameter values.

concepts.name: 12 Layers
concepts.summary: The stack is twelve decoder blocks deep, and the analysis section treats that depth as a dial the transfer experiments turn.
concepts.explanation:
Depth here is the number of identical decoder blocks stacked between the embeddings and the output.

Twelve is the paper's choice for pre-training.

It is also the quantity the layer-transfer experiment sweeps. Transferring zero layers means keeping only the embeddings; full transfer means carrying all twelve into the fine-tuned model.

So the number is more than a size setting. It sets the resolution of the analysis curve, which reports performance for each count of layers carried over.

concepts.name: 768-Dimensional States
concepts.summary: Each token is represented by a 768-dimensional vector at every layer of the stack.
concepts.explanation:
The model width is 768. Every token embedding, every layer output and every residual stream vector has that many components.

Width is what the residual connections force to stay constant: because each sublayer adds its output back onto its input, the two must have the same size all the way up.

It also interacts with the head count. Splitting 768 across 12 attention heads gives each head $768/12 = 64$ dimensions to work in.

concepts.name: 12 Attention Heads
concepts.summary: Each layer's self-attention is split into twelve parallel heads, each attending in a 64-dimensional subspace.
concepts.explanation:
Multi-head attention runs several attention operations side by side instead of one wide one. Each head projects the 768-dimensional state into a smaller subspace, attends there, and the outputs are concatenated back.

With 12 heads over 768 dimensions, each head works in $768/12 = 64$ dimensions, and twelve 64-dimensional outputs restore the full width.

Every one of these heads is masked, so all twelve see only the current position and earlier ones.

concepts.name: 3072-Dimensional Inner Feed-Forward States
concepts.summary: The feed-forward sublayer in each block expands from 768 to 3072 dimensions and projects back down.
concepts.explanation:
After attention, each block passes every position independently through a small two-layer network. Position-wise means the same network is applied to each token's vector separately, with no mixing across positions.

The paper sets the inner width to 3072. So the sublayer projects $768 \rightarrow 3072$, applies its nonlinearity, then projects $3072 \rightarrow 768$ to restore the residual width.

That is a factor of four expansion in the middle.

The nonlinearity applied at the 3072-dimensional point is [[gelu]].

concepts.name: Gaussian Error Linear Unit (GELU)
concepts.summary: The activation function used in place of ReLU. It gates each input by the probability that a standard normal draw falls below it.
concepts.explanation:
A ReLU makes a hard decision: keep the input if it is positive, otherwise output zero. GELU makes the same decision smoothly.

It multiplies the input by the standard normal cumulative distribution function evaluated at that input, $\mathrm{GELU}(x) = x\,\Phi(x)$.

A large positive input passes through almost unchanged, because $\Phi(x)$ is near 1. A large negative input is suppressed, because $\Phi(x)$ is near 0. Inputs near zero are scaled by something in between rather than snapped to one side.

The paper adopts it without argument, as one line in the specification. It appears at the 3072-dimensional point inside every position-wise feed-forward sublayer.

citedFrom.refText: D. Hendrycks and K. Gimpel. Bridging nonlinearities and stochastic regularizers with gaussian error linear units. arXiv:1606.08415, 2016.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The activation is defined and motivated there; this paper only names it.

concepts.name: Layer Normalization
concepts.summary: Per-position normalization of activations to zero mean and unit variance, with learned gain and bias. Used throughout the stack.
concepts.explanation:
Layer normalization rescales each position's activation vector using statistics computed over that vector's own components, then applies a learned gain and bias.

The paper treats it as standard equipment and notes only how heavily it is used.

The consequence that matters in the setup section is that layernorm sits between the layers everywhere, which is the reason the paper gives for its simple [[weight-initialization]].

citedFrom.refText: J. L. Ba, J. R. Kiros, and G. E. Hinton. Layer normalization. arXiv:1607.06450, 2016.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: Definition of the normalization scheme the setup relies on.

concepts.name: $\mathcal{N}(0, 0.02)$ Weight Initialization
concepts.summary: All weights are drawn from a normal distribution with standard deviation 0.02, which the paper says was sufficient because layernorm is used throughout.
concepts.explanation:
Deep stacks are usually sensitive to initialization scale, because activations can grow or shrink multiplicatively as they pass through many layers.

The paper reports it did not need a scale-aware scheme. Weights are sampled from $\mathcal{N}(0, 0.02)$.

Its stated reason is layer normalization: because activations are renormalized at every layer, the scale drift that initialization schemes are designed to prevent is corrected as it arises.

This is reported as an observation about what worked, not as an analysis.

concepts.name: Pre-Training Optimization Setup
concepts.summary: How the language model was actually trained: Adam, a warmup-then-cosine schedule peaking at 2.5e-4, and 100 epochs of 64-sequence minibatches.
concepts.explanation:
The setup section fixes the optimizer and its schedule as tightly as it fixes the architecture.

Updates use Adam. The learning rate does not start at its maximum: it rises linearly from zero over the first 2000 updates, peaks at 2.5e-4, then decays to zero along a cosine curve for the rest of training.

Training runs for 100 epochs over BooksCorpus. Each minibatch holds 64 sequences, and each sequence is a contiguous 512-token span sampled at random from the corpus.

These are the numbers a reader would need to reproduce the pre-trained model that everything else in the paper starts from.

concepts.name: Adam Optimizer
concepts.summary: The adaptive gradient method used for pre-training, with a maximum learning rate of 2.5e-4.
concepts.explanation:
Adam keeps running averages of both the gradient and its square for each parameter, and divides the step by the square root of the second average.

The practical effect is a per-parameter step size. Parameters with consistently large gradients take proportionally smaller steps, so one global learning rate can serve very differently scaled parameters.

This paper sets that global rate's ceiling at 2.5e-4 for pre-training. It is a ceiling rather than a constant because the schedule warms up to it and then anneals away from it.

Adam also matters for the weight decay choice, since the [[decoupled-weight-decay|modified L2 regularization]] the paper adopts is a fix specific to how decay interacts with Adam's adaptive denominator.

citedFrom.refText: D. P. Kingma and J. Ba. Adam: a method for stochastic optimization. arXiv:1412.6980, 2014.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The update rule, its moment estimates and default betas are defined there and are needed to reproduce the schedule.

concepts.name: Linear Warmup Over 2000 Updates
concepts.summary: The learning rate is raised linearly from zero to 2.5e-4 across the first 2000 updates instead of starting at full size.
concepts.explanation:
At the very start of training the parameters are random and Adam's running estimates of gradient scale rest on almost no data.

Taking full-size steps in that regime can push the model somewhere it takes a long time to recover from. Warmup avoids the question by making the early steps small.

The schedule is linear in the update count: update 1 uses a rate near zero, update 2000 uses the full 2.5e-4, and the rate rises in equal increments in between.

Only after those 2000 updates does the annealing phase begin.

concepts.name: Cosine Learning Rate Annealing
concepts.summary: After warmup, the learning rate follows a cosine curve from 2.5e-4 down to zero over the remainder of training.
concepts.explanation:
Once warmup ends the rate is decayed rather than held fixed. The paper anneals it to 0 on a cosine schedule.

The shape of that curve is the point. A cosine falling from peak to trough is nearly flat at first, steepest in the middle, and nearly flat again at the end.

So the model spends a long stretch training near the maximum rate, then gets a long gentle tail of very small steps.

Training ends with the learning rate at zero, meaning the final parameters are settled rather than still moving.

concepts.name: 100 Epochs of 64-Sequence Minibatches
concepts.summary: Pre-training makes 100 passes over BooksCorpus with minibatches of 64 randomly sampled contiguous sequences.
concepts.explanation:
An epoch is one pass over the corpus, and the paper takes 100 of them.

Each gradient step uses 64 sequences at once. The sequences are sampled at random from the corpus, but each is contiguous internally — a real 512-token span of a real book, not a bag of unrelated sentences.

Multiplying out, a single minibatch supplies $64 \times 512 = 32{,}768$ tokens. Because [[masked-self-attention|masked self-attention]] lets every position be a prediction target, essentially all of them contribute a next-token loss term in one forward pass.

The schedule also anchors the warmup figure: 2000 updates is a small slice of a 100-epoch run.

concepts.name: 512-Token Context Window
concepts.summary: The window $k$ of preceding tokens a prediction may condition on, fixed at 512 contiguous tokens in the trained model.
concepts.explanation:
In $L_1$ the conditioning set is written out as $u_{i-k},\dots,u_{i-1}$, so $k$ fixes how far back the model may look when predicting token $i$.

A larger $k$ lets the model condition on longer-range structure. It also costs more computation, since self-attention compares every position in the window against every other.

Section 4.1 trains on contiguous spans of 512 tokens, so that is the window the model actually sees. Nothing outside it is visible to attention.

Because the span is contiguous, those 512 slots hold several paragraphs of one book. A shuffled corpus would fill the same slots with unrelated sentences.

The number also fixes the height of the learned position embedding table, since there must be one trained vector per slot. And it caps what any downstream task can present, because fine-tuning reuses the same window for its transformed inputs.

concepts.name: Regularization Setup
concepts.summary: Three regularizers during pre-training: dropout at 0.1 in three places, a modified L2 weight decay at $w = 0.01$, and no decay on biases or gains.
concepts.explanation:
The paper trains a 12-layer model for 100 epochs on a fixed corpus, so it states its defences against overfitting explicitly.

Dropout is applied at rate 0.1 in three distinct places: on the residual connections, on the embeddings, and inside attention.

Separately, a modified version of L2 regularization pulls weights towards zero with coefficient $w = 0.01$, applied to all weights except biases and gains.

The exemption is deliberate. Biases and layernorm gains are few in number and set operating points rather than input-output mappings, so shrinking them regularizes little and distorts normalization.

concepts.name: Dropout
concepts.summary: Randomly zeroing activations during training to discourage co-adaptation. Assumed known.
concepts.explanation:
During training a fraction of units is set to zero at random on each forward pass, so no unit can rely on any particular other unit being present.

This paper assumes the idea and specifies only rates and placement.

concepts.name: Residual, Embedding and Attention Dropout at 0.1
concepts.summary: Dropout with rate 0.1 applied at three points: residual branches, the embedding layer, and attention.
concepts.explanation:
The paper does not apply one blanket dropout; it names three sites.

Residual dropout drops activations on a sublayer's output before it is added back onto the residual stream. Embedding dropout drops components of the summed token and position embeddings at the bottom of the stack. Attention dropout drops entries of the attention distribution itself, so a head cannot depend on one specific source position.

All three use the same rate of 0.1, meaning one value in ten is zeroed on each training pass.

The same rate is reused for a fresh dropout on the classifier during fine-tuning.

concepts.name: Modified L2 Regularization (Decoupled Weight Decay)
concepts.summary: A variant of L2 regularization designed for Adam, applied with $w = 0.01$ to all non-bias and non-gain weights.
concepts.explanation:
Classical L2 regularization adds a penalty term to the loss, so its gradient flows through the optimizer like any other gradient.

With Adam that has a side effect. Adam divides every gradient component by its own running root-mean-square, so the penalty on a parameter with large gradients is scaled down while the penalty on a quiet parameter is scaled up.

The intended uniform pull towards zero therefore becomes uneven.

The modified version the paper adopts decouples the two. The decay is applied directly to the weights as a separate shrinkage step, outside Adam's adaptive rescaling, so the strength $w = 0.01$ means the same thing for every parameter it touches.

citedFrom.refText: I. Loshchilov and F. Hutter. Fixing weight decay regularization in adam. arXiv:1711.05101, 2017.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The exact modified update rule, and why L2 and weight decay differ under Adam, live there; this section only names it and gives w.

concepts.name: Text Preprocessing Pipeline
concepts.summary: Raw BooksCorpus text is cleaned with ftfy, tokenized with spaCy, then converted to subword units by byte-pair encoding with 40,000 merges.
concepts.explanation:
Between the raw books and the model sits a three-stage pipeline, and the paper names each stage.

First ftfy repairs mangled text and standardizes some punctuation and whitespace. Then the [[spacy-tokenizer]] splits the cleaned text into word-level tokens.

Finally byte-pair encoding maps those tokens into a subword vocabulary built with 40,000 merges. That is the unit the model actually sees, and the unit the reported perplexity of 18.4 is averaged over.

The order matters. BPE learns its merges from whatever the earlier stages produce, so encoding noise and inconsistent whitespace would otherwise be baked into the vocabulary.

concepts.name: ftfy
concepts.summary: A library used to clean the raw BooksCorpus text and standardize some punctuation and whitespace.
concepts.explanation:
Text scraped from the wild carries encoding damage: characters decoded under the wrong codec, stray control characters, curly and straight quotes used interchangeably.

The paper runs ftfy over raw BooksCorpus to repair this.

The reason to bother is downstream. Every distinct surface form is a separate thing for the tokenizer and for BPE to learn, so leaving three spellings of a quotation mark in the corpus spends vocabulary on an artefact of encoding.

concepts.name: spaCy Tokenizer
concepts.summary: The word-level tokenizer applied to the cleaned text before byte-pair encoding.
concepts.explanation:
Tokenization here is the step that decides where one word ends and the next begins, including how to treat punctuation, contractions and hyphens.

The paper uses spaCy's tokenizer for this, and its output is a stream of word-level tokens.

Those tokens are not what the model consumes. They are the input to byte-pair encoding, which then breaks rare ones into subword pieces.

concepts.name: Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE)
concepts.summary: A subword vocabulary built by repeatedly merging the most frequent adjacent symbol pair, so common words stay whole and rare words split into pieces.
concepts.explanation:
BPE starts from a vocabulary of individual characters, so at the outset every word is spelled out one character at a time.

It then counts adjacent symbol pairs across the corpus and merges the most frequent pair into a single new symbol. Repeating this grows the vocabulary by one entry per merge.

Because merges follow frequency, common sequences fuse early. A word like the becomes a single symbol quickly, while a rare proper noun is left as several pieces.

The payoff is that there is no out-of-vocabulary token. Any string can be spelled from pieces already in the vocabulary, down to single characters in the worst case.

The cost is that a rare word occupies several positions in the 512-token window rather than one.

citedFrom.refText: R. Sennrich, B. Haddow, and A. Birch. Neural machine translation of rare words with subword units. arXiv:1508.07909, 2015.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The merge algorithm and its training procedure are defined there; this paper gives only the merge count.

concepts.name: 40,000 Merges
concepts.summary: The number of merge operations used to build the vocabulary, the single knob controlling how coarse the subword units are.
concepts.explanation:
Each merge adds one symbol, so 40,000 merges gives a vocabulary of roughly that size on top of the initial character set.

The count trades off two costs. Too few merges and common words stay fragmented, so the 512-token window holds less text and the model must reassemble words at every layer.

Too many and the vocabulary grows large, inflating the embedding table and the output softmax while the extra entries cover ever rarer strings.

At 40,000 merges the frequent English vocabulary of BooksCorpus is largely whole-word and the tail is handled by pieces.

This is also why the reported 18.4 is a token-level perplexity: the averaging unit is one of these subword symbols, not a word.

concepts.name: Fine-Tuning Hyperparameters
concepts.summary: Fine-tuning reuses the pre-training settings except for a learning rate of 6.25e-5, batch size 32, three epochs, classifier dropout 0.1, and a short warmup.
concepts.explanation:
The paper's stated default is inheritance: unless it says otherwise, the fine-tuning run keeps the pre-training hyperparameters.

The exceptions are small. A fresh dropout at rate 0.1 is added to the classifier head. Most tasks use a learning rate of 6.25e-5, roughly a quarter of the pre-training maximum, with a batch size of 32.

Training is short. The paper reports that the model finetunes quickly and that 3 epochs sufficed for most cases.

The schedule is linear decay with warmup over 0.2% of training, and the [[auxiliary-lm-objective|auxiliary language modelling objective]] is weighted at $\lambda = 0.5$.

The short, low-rate schedule is part of the paper's claim that adapting a pre-trained model to a task is cheap compared with training one. Note the hedge: most cases, not all.

concepts.name: Classifier Dropout
concepts.summary: An extra dropout at rate 0.1 applied to the task-specific classifier head added during fine-tuning.
concepts.explanation:
Fine-tuning attaches a small linear output layer on top of the transformer for each task.

That head is freshly initialized and trained on a labelled dataset that may hold only a few thousand examples, which makes it the most overfitting-prone part of the model.

So the paper adds dropout to it at rate 0.1, matching the rate used inside the pre-trained stack.

concepts.name: Learning Rate 6.25e-5, Batch Size 32
concepts.summary: The optimization settings used for most fine-tuning runs, notably a learning rate about four times smaller than pre-training's peak.
concepts.explanation:
Fine-tuning starts from parameters that already encode a working language model, so the goal is adjustment rather than learning from scratch.

The paper reflects this in the rate. Where pre-training peaked at 2.5e-4, most fine-tuning runs use 6.25e-5, a quarter of that.

A smaller rate means smaller steps, so the pre-trained solution is nudged rather than overwritten. The batch is also halved, from 64 sequences to 32.

The hedge in the paper is worth keeping: it says most tasks, so some datasets used other values.

concepts.name: Three Epochs of Fine-Tuning
concepts.summary: The paper reports that three passes over a task's training set were enough for most datasets.
concepts.explanation:
Pre-training runs for 100 epochs; fine-tuning runs for 3.

The paper offers this as an observation about speed — the model finetunes quickly, and 3 epochs was sufficient for most cases.

Read alongside the pre-training figure, it is the cheapness argument in numbers. One expensive unsupervised run is amortized across twelve datasets, each costing three short passes.

Again the claim is hedged with most cases rather than stated for all tasks.

concepts.name: Linear Decay with 0.2% Warmup
concepts.summary: During fine-tuning the learning rate warms up over the first 0.2% of updates, then decays linearly to zero.
concepts.explanation:
Fine-tuning uses a different schedule shape from pre-training's cosine.

There is still a warmup, but a very short one: 0.2% of total updates, which over a three-epoch run is a handful of steps.

After that the rate falls linearly to zero across the remaining updates.

The brief warmup does the same job as before, letting the freshly initialized classifier head take small steps before full-size updates start propagating into the pre-trained weights below it.

concepts.name: Four Task Families, Twelve Datasets
concepts.summary: The paper evaluates on natural language inference, question answering and commonsense reasoning, semantic similarity, and text classification, across twelve datasets.
concepts.explanation:
Rather than tuning one benchmark, the paper spreads evaluation across four families of supervised task.

Twelve datasets sit under them, some drawn from the GLUE multi-task benchmark.

The spread is the argument. A single model with one architecture and one pre-training run is fine-tuned on each, with only the input transformation and the output head changing.

The headline is new state-of-the-art results on 9 of the 12 datasets, in many cases beating ensembles.

The paper also notes the datasets span sizes from roughly 5.7k training examples on STS-B up to roughly 550k on SNLI, and uses that range to claim the method is not just a large-data technique.

concepts.name: Absolute Improvement
concepts.summary: The paper reports its gains as differences in percentage points against the previous best, not as relative reductions in error.
concepts.explanation:
There are two ways to report an improvement. A relative figure divides the gain by the previous score or the previous error. An absolute figure just subtracts.

The paper is explicit that its headline numbers are absolute: 8.9% on Story Cloze, 5.7% on RACE, 1.5% on MultiNLI and 5.5% on GLUE.

So an 8.9% absolute gain means accuracy moved by 8.9 points, which on a task already scoring high is a large shift.

The reporting style matters when comparing these numbers against figures quoted elsewhere.

concepts.name: 9 of 12 Datasets
concepts.summary: The paper's headline count: new best published results on nine of the twelve datasets, in many cases beating ensembles.
concepts.explanation:
Rather than a single benchmark number, the summary statistic is a count across the evaluation suite.

The paper reports new state-of-the-art results on 9 out of the 12 datasets, outperforming ensembles in many cases.

The three it does not claim are visible in the section text: RTE, where it trails a multi-task biLSTM, SST-2, where it calls its result competitive rather than best, and one of the three [[semantic-similarity]] datasets.

Read carefully, the count also concedes that three specialised systems were not beaten.

concepts.name: GLUE Benchmark
concepts.summary: A recently released multi-task benchmark bundling several language understanding datasets, from which the paper draws some tasks and reports an overall score of 72.8.
concepts.explanation:
GLUE collects existing language understanding datasets under one evaluation harness, so a single model can be scored across all of them and summarized by one aggregate number.

The paper says some of its tasks are available as part of this benchmark.

It reports an overall GLUE score of 72.8 against a previous best of 68.9, a 5.5% [[absolute-improvement]]. Because the aggregate mixes tasks with different metrics and sizes, it is a summary of breadth rather than a measurement of any one capability.

The introduction also points at the GLUE leaderboard in a footnote, as evidence that different pre-training objectives win on different tasks.

citedFrom.refText: A. Wang, A. Singh, J. Michael, F. Hill, O. Levy, and S. R. Bowman. Glue: a multi-task benchmark and analysis platform for natural language understanding. arXiv:1804.07461, 2018.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: Which datasets GLUE contains and how the aggregate score is computed are defined there.
