concepts.name: Baselines and Ensembles
concepts.summary: The prior systems measured against: mostly task-specific biLSTM architectures, sometimes with ELMo features, attention, or ensembling.
concepts.explanation:
The comparison points in these tables are the previous best result on each dataset, which at this point are mostly bidirectional LSTM models designed for one task.

Two are named directly. A multi-task biLSTM model holds the RTE result of 61.7% the paper does not beat. A Single-task BiLSTM + ELMo + Attn model is the [[qqp]] baseline it improves on by 4.2%.

Some baselines are ensembles — several models whose predictions are combined, which usually costs several times the compute of a single model.

The paper notes that its single fine-tuned model outperforms ensembles in many cases, which is part of its argument that one pre-trained model plus light adaptation can replace bespoke architectures.

concepts.name: LSTM
concepts.summary: A recurrent architecture that processes tokens in sequence through a gated hidden state. Assumed known; used here as the comparison architecture.
concepts.explanation:
An LSTM reads a sequence one position at a time, carrying a hidden state forward and using gates to control what is kept and what is overwritten.

The paper assumes this and uses LSTMs in two roles: as the backbone of most prior state-of-the-art baselines, and as the substitute architecture in its own ablation and zero-shot comparisons.

concepts.name: Natural Language Inference (Textual Entailment)
concepts.summary: Given a premise and a hypothesis, decide whether the premise entails the hypothesis, contradicts it, or leaves it open.
concepts.explanation:
An NLI example is a pair of texts. The first is the premise and the second the hypothesis, and the label describes the relation from premise to hypothesis.

Entailment means a reader accepting the premise would accept the hypothesis. Contradiction means accepting the premise rules the hypothesis out. Neutral means the premise leaves the question open.

The ordering is part of the problem, which is why the entailment transformation can concatenate the two in a fixed order and stop there.

The paper notes the task has attracted recent interest but remains challenging, because a decision can require lexical entailment — one word naming a subtype of another — plus coreference resolution and the resolution of lexical and syntactic ambiguity.

It evaluates on five NLI datasets deliberately drawn from different sources: image captions, transcribed speech, fiction, government reports, Wikipedia, science exams and news. Success is therefore not a property of one text domain.

concepts.name: Coreference
concepts.summary: Two expressions in a text referring to the same entity, for instance a pronoun and the name it stands for.
concepts.explanation:
Coreference is the link between a mention and what it refers to. A pronoun, a definite description like the doctor, and a proper name can all point at one entity.

An NLI system has to resolve these links before it can compare premise with hypothesis, because the two sentences may name the same entity in different ways.

The paper lists coreference among the phenomena that make NLI difficult. It returns in the analysis section, where the DPRD zero-shot heuristic is a coreference problem in its own right.

concepts.name: SNLI
concepts.summary: A large NLI dataset built from image captions; the biggest in the evaluation at roughly 550k training examples.
concepts.explanation:
SNLI draws its premises from image captions, so the sentences describe concrete visual scenes.

At roughly 550,000 training examples it is the largest of the twelve datasets.

The paper reports an [[absolute-improvement]] of 0.6% over the previous best here — the smallest of its NLI gains, on the dataset where prior supervised methods already had the most labelled data.

SNLI is also one end of the size argument, used against STS-B to claim the approach works across dataset sizes.

citedFrom.refText: S. R. Bowman, G. Angeli, C. Potts, and C. D. Manning. A large annotated corpus for learning natural language inference. EMNLP, 2015.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The dataset's construction, label scheme and split sizes are defined there.

concepts.name: MultiNLI (MNLI)
concepts.summary: A multi-genre NLI dataset covering transcribed speech, popular fiction and government reports, used as a benchmark and in the layer-transfer analysis.
concepts.explanation:
MultiNLI keeps SNLI's three-way label scheme but widens the source material across genres.

The genre spread is the point. A model cannot succeed by learning the register of one text source.

The paper reports an [[absolute-improvement]] of up to 1.5% over the previous best, one of the three headline numbers quoted in the abstract.

MultiNLI does double duty. It is also one of the two tasks plotted in the layer-transfer analysis, where transferring all twelve layers is worth up to 9% over transferring embeddings alone.

citedFrom.refText: A. Williams, N. Nangia, and S. R. Bowman. A broad-coverage challenge corpus for sentence understanding through inference. NAACL, 2018.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The genre composition and matched/mismatched split structure are defined there.

concepts.name: QNLI
concepts.summary: An NLI dataset built over Wikipedia articles, where the paper reports its largest NLI gain at 5.8%.
concepts.explanation:
QNLI presents the entailment task over text drawn from Wikipedia articles.

It is handled like the other four NLI datasets, through the sentence-pair input transformation and a classifier head.

The paper reports an [[absolute-improvement]] of 5.8% over the previous best result, the largest of its five NLI margins.

QNLI is one of the datasets taken from the [[glue-benchmark]].

concepts.name: SciTail
concepts.summary: An entailment dataset built from science exam questions, on which the paper reports a 5% absolute improvement.
concepts.explanation:
SciTail poses the entailment task over material from science exams, so premises and hypotheses carry technical content rather than everyday description.

It is one of the five NLI datasets, chosen as part of the deliberate spread of text sources.

The paper reports an [[absolute-improvement]] of 5% over the previous best result.

citedFrom.refText: T. Khot, A. Sabharwal, and P. Clark. Scitail: a textual entailment dataset from science question answering. AAAI, 2018.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: How entailment pairs were derived from science questions is defined there.

concepts.name: RTE
concepts.summary: A small NLI dataset over news articles, with 2490 training examples, and the one NLI dataset where the paper does not beat the previous best.
concepts.explanation:
RTE is the smallest NLI dataset in the evaluation, with 2490 training examples drawn from news articles.

Here the model reaches 56% accuracy, below the 61.7% reported by a multi-task biLSTM model. The paper states this plainly rather than working around it.

Its explanation is size plus training regime. Given strong performance on the larger NLI datasets, it says it is likely the model would benefit from multi-task training as well.

That last clause is worth keeping as written, together with the admission that it has not explored this. The multi-task explanation is a conjecture the paper offers, not something it tests.

citedFrom.refText: L. Bentivogli, P. Clark, I. Dagan, and D. Giampiccolo. The fifth pascal recognizing textual entailment challenge. TAC, 2009.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The RTE challenge data and its label conventions are defined there.

concepts.name: Question Answering and Commonsense Reasoning
concepts.summary: Tasks requiring single- and multi-sentence reasoning over a passage: the paper evaluates on RACE and the Story Cloze Test.
concepts.explanation:
This family asks the model to read a passage and select an answer, which needs reasoning that spans sentences rather than matching one.

Commonsense reasoning is the harder end of it. Those problems cannot be settled by matching text against text; they need expectations about ordinary events — what usually follows what, what people typically want.

Both datasets are handled through the multiple-choice input transformation. The passage and question are concatenated with each candidate answer in turn, and the candidates are scored against each other.

The paper reports gains of up to 8.9% on Story Cloze and 5.7% overall on RACE, and reads these as evidence the model handles long-range contexts effectively.

concepts.name: RACE
concepts.summary: A reading comprehension dataset of English exam passages and questions, chosen because it contains more reasoning-type questions than the alternatives.
concepts.explanation:
RACE collects passages and multiple-choice questions from middle-school and high-school English examinations.

The paper's reason for choosing it is the question mix. It states that the corpus has been shown to contain more reasoning-type questions than datasets like CNN or SQuAD, which makes it a test of inference rather than of span matching.

Since exam passages are long and the answer is often not local, the paper calls it a good fit for a model trained to handle long-range contexts, and reports a 5.7% overall improvement.

RACE returns twice more. It is one of the two curves in the layer-transfer plot, and one of the four zero-shot heuristics is built for it.

citedFrom.refText: G. Lai, Q. Xie, H. Liu, Y. Yang, and E. Hovy. Race: large-scale reading comprehension dataset from examinations. EMNLP, 2017.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: Passage length, question types, and the analysis showing it is more reasoning-heavy than CNN or SQuAD are established there.

concepts.name: CNN and SQuAD as Contrast Datasets
concepts.summary: Two earlier reading comprehension datasets named only to argue that RACE demands more reasoning than they do.
concepts.explanation:
The paper does not evaluate on CNN or SQuAD. It mentions them to position RACE.

Both are established reading comprehension datasets in which answers are typically found in the passage, often as a span to be located rather than a conclusion to be drawn.

The claim is that RACE has been shown to contain more reasoning-type questions than these.

Note the hedge in the phrasing. The paper cites this as an established finding about RACE rather than demonstrating it here.

citedFrom.refText: [19] K. M. Hermann et al. Teaching machines to read and comprehend. NIPS 2015. [47] P. Rajpurkar, J. Zhang, K. Lopyrev, and P. Liang. Squad: 100,000+ questions for machine comprehension of text. EMNLP, 2016.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The comparison rests on what these datasets' questions look like, which is only established in those papers.

concepts.name: Story Cloze Test
concepts.summary: A commonsense task: given a multi-sentence story, choose the correct ending from two options.
concepts.explanation:
Each item gives a short everyday narrative followed by two candidate final sentences, exactly one of which is the real ending.

Both endings are written to be locally plausible, so word overlap alone does not settle it. Choosing correctly usually needs expectations about how situations resolve.

The paper reports an improvement of up to 8.9% over the previous best, its single largest margin and the number most often quoted from the abstract.

The two-option format maps directly onto the multiple-choice transformation: build one sequence per ending and compare their scores. This result is also the strongest support offered for the claim that pre-training on contiguous prose supplies [[world-knowledge]].

citedFrom.refText: N. Mostafazadeh, M. Roth, A. Louis, N. Chambers, and J. Allen. Lsdsem 2017 shared task: the story cloze test. 2017.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The shared-task setup, how the wrong endings were written, and the evaluation split are defined there.

concepts.name: Semantic Similarity
concepts.summary: Deciding whether two sentences mean the same thing, also called paraphrase detection. Evaluated on MRPC, QQP and STS-B.
concepts.explanation:
Semantic similarity asks whether two sentences are semantically equivalent, however differently they are worded. Some datasets want a binary answer, others a graded score.

The paper lists three difficulties: recognizing rephrasing of concepts, understanding negation, and handling syntactic ambiguity. Negation is the sharp one, since inserting a single not can flip meaning while leaving almost every word intact.

The relation is symmetric: if A paraphrases B then B paraphrases A. Section 3.3 makes the same point by saying there is no inherent ordering of the two sentences.

That symmetry is what the [[similarity-input-transformation]] is built to satisfy.

The paper reports state-of-the-art results on two of the three datasets: a 1 point absolute gain on STS-B and a 4.2% [[absolute-improvement]] on [[qqp]].

concepts.name: Microsoft Paraphrase Corpus (MRPC)
concepts.summary: A paraphrase detection dataset collected from news sources; the one dataset where the LSTM ablation beats the transformer.
concepts.explanation:
MRPC pairs sentences collected from news sources and labels whether each pair is a paraphrase.

It is one of three [[semantic-similarity]] datasets, and one of the two in this family on which the paper does not report a new state of the art.

MRPC shows up again in the ablations. When the transformer is swapped for a single-layer 2048-unit LSTM, MRPC is the only dataset where the LSTM comes out ahead.

The paper records that exception without explaining it.

citedFrom.refText: W. B. Dolan and C. Brockett. Automatically constructing a corpus of sentential paraphrases. IWP2005.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The corpus construction and its paraphrase labelling criteria are defined there.

concepts.name: Quora Question Pairs (QQP)
concepts.summary: A dataset of question pairs labelled for whether they ask the same thing, where the paper reports a 4.2% absolute improvement.
concepts.explanation:
QQP consists of pairs of questions posted to Quora, labelled according to whether the two ask the same thing.

The paper calls its margin here significant: a 4.2% [[absolute-improvement]] over a Single-task BiLSTM + ELMo + Attn baseline.

QQP also appears in the first ablation. It is one of the datasets, alongside the NLI tasks, where dropping the [[auxiliary-lm-objective|auxiliary language modelling objective]] hurts.

That is consistent with the paper's reading that larger datasets benefit from that objective.

citedFrom.refText: Z. Chen, H. Zhang, X. Zhang, and L. Zhao. Quora question pairs. 2018.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The dataset release, size and labelling are defined there, and the size is needed for the 'larger datasets benefit' claim.

concepts.name: Semantic Textual Similarity Benchmark (STS-B)
concepts.summary: A semantic similarity dataset of roughly 5.7k training examples, the smallest in the evaluation, where the paper reports a 1 point absolute gain.
concepts.explanation:
STS-B scores how semantically close two sentences are, on a graded scale rather than a binary label.

The paper reports a 1 point absolute gain over the previous best.

Its other role is as the small end of the size range. With roughly 5,700 training examples it anchors the claim that the approach works across datasets of different sizes, against SNLI's roughly 550,000 at the other end.

That range spans about two orders of magnitude, which is the basis for the paper's claim of robustness to dataset size.

citedFrom.refText: D. Cer, M. Diab, E. Agirre, I. Lopez-Gazpio, and L. Specia. Semeval-2017 task 1: semantic textual similarity. arXiv:1708.00055, 2017.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The similarity rating scale and correlation metric a '1 point absolute gain' is measured on are defined there.

concepts.name: Text Classification
concepts.summary: Single-sentence labelling tasks: CoLA for grammatical acceptability and SST-2 for binary sentiment.
concepts.explanation:
This family takes one input sequence and returns one label, with no second sentence to compare against.

It is the simplest of the four types, because the input needs no restructuring beyond the [[start-and-end-tokens]] to be fed to a language model.

That simplicity is why earlier pre-training work stopped there: both closest predecessors demonstrated language-model pre-training on classification alone.

The results here split. CoLA jumps to 45.4 from a previous best of 35.0, which the paper reads as evidence of learned linguistic bias, while SST-2 reaches 91.3% accuracy, which it calls competitive with the state of the art rather than better.

concepts.name: Corpus of Linguistic Acceptability (CoLA)
concepts.summary: Expert judgements on whether a sentence is grammatical. The paper reports a score of 45.4 against a previous best of 35.0.
concepts.explanation:
CoLA contains sentences labelled by experts as grammatical or not, so the task probes syntax rather than content.

The paper describes it as testing the innate linguistic bias of trained models — whether a model has internalized what well-formed English looks like.

It reports 45.4, calls this an especially big jump over the previous best of 35.0, and reads the jump as showcasing linguistic bias learned during pre-training.

That reading is an interpretation offered on top of one number, not a controlled test of it.

CoLA also reappears as one of the four zero-shot heuristics in the analysis.

citedFrom.refText: A. Warstadt, A. Singh, and S. R. Bowman. Corpus of linguistic acceptability. 2018.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The acceptability judgements and the correlation metric the 45.4 is measured in are defined there.

concepts.name: Stanford Sentiment Treebank (SST-2)
concepts.summary: A binary sentiment classification task, on which the paper reports 91.3% accuracy, competitive with but not beating the state of the art.
concepts.explanation:
SST-2 labels sentences as positive or negative in sentiment, which the paper calls a standard binary classification task.

The model reaches 91.3% accuracy.

The paper describes this as competitive with the state-of-the-art results rather than as a new best, making it one of the three datasets out of twelve where it does not claim the top result.

SST-2 also supplies one of the zero-shot heuristics, where sentiment is read off the language model directly.

citedFrom.refText: R. Socher, A. Perelygin, J. Wu, J. Chuang, C. D. Manning, A. Ng, and C. Potts. Recursive deep models for semantic compositionality over a sentiment treebank. EMNLP, 2013.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The treebank and its binary sentence-level split define what 91.3% accuracy is measured on, and the label vocabulary underpins the zero-shot heuristic.

concepts.name: Impact of Number of Layers Transferred
concepts.summary: An analysis varying how many pre-trained layers are carried into fine-tuning, showing each transformer layer adds performance, up to 9% on MultiNLI for full transfer.
concepts.explanation:
After pre-training, the paper can choose how much of the model to carry into the supervised task. Transfer zero layers and only the embeddings come across; transfer all twelve and the whole stack does.

The analysis sweeps that count on MultiNLI and RACE and plots performance against it.

Two things come out. Transferring embeddings helps, which the paper calls the standard result and which matches years of word-vector practice.

Beyond that, each additional transformer layer keeps adding, up to 9% for full transfer on MultiNLI.

The paper's reading is that each layer of the pre-trained model contains useful functionality for solving target tasks, not just the bottom embedding layer. That is the argument against treating pre-training as a source of word vectors only.

concepts.name: Zero-Shot Behaviours
concepts.summary: Heuristics that make the pre-trained generative model perform the evaluation tasks with no supervised fine-tuning at all, tracked across pre-training.
concepts.explanation:
The paper wants to know why language model pre-training of transformers works, and puts forward a hypothesis: the generative model learns to perform many of the evaluation tasks in the course of improving its language modelling.

To test this it strips out the supervised part entirely. It designs one heuristic per task that reads an answer directly off the generative model, with no fine-tuning and no trained classifier head.

It then runs those heuristics at checkpoints across pre-training and plots how they do as a function of updates.

The reported pattern is that performance is stable and steadily increases, which the paper takes as evidence that pre-training builds task-relevant functionality rather than fine-tuning acquiring it.

The same heuristics are also run against an LSTM, which the paper reports shows higher variance in zero-shot performance.

These are heuristics the authors designed, so the absolute numbers say as much about the heuristic as about the model. The trend across updates is what the paper actually leans on.

concepts.name: Average Token Log-Probability Scoring
concepts.summary: The common device behind three of the four heuristics: score a candidate string by the mean log-probability the language model assigns its tokens.
concepts.explanation:
A language model returns a probability for each token given the tokens before it. Summing the logs of those probabilities gives a score for a whole string.

Dividing by the number of tokens gives the average.

That normalization matters when candidates differ in length, because a longer string accumulates more negative log-probability simply by being longer and would otherwise always lose.

With this in hand, choosing between candidates becomes a comparison of numbers. CoLA thresholds a single score; RACE and DPRD compare scores across candidates.

No training is involved. The score is read straight from the pre-trained model.

concepts.name: CoLA Zero-Shot Heuristic
concepts.summary: Score each sentence by the generative model's average token log-probability and predict acceptability by thresholding that score.
concepts.explanation:
CoLA asks whether a sentence is grammatical, and the heuristic answers with fluency.

Each example is scored as the average token log-probability the generative model assigns it. An ungrammatical sentence should contain at least one token the model finds unlikely in its context, dragging the average down.

A threshold on that single number produces the binary prediction.

This is the simplest of the four heuristics: no substitution, no candidate comparison, just one score and a cut point.

concepts.name: SST-2 Zero-Shot Heuristic
concepts.summary: Append the token 'very' to the example, restrict the output distribution to 'positive' and 'negative', and take whichever scores higher.
concepts.explanation:
This heuristic turns sentiment classification into a next-token prediction.

The token very is appended to the example, setting up a continuation where an intensifier is naturally followed by an evaluative adjective.

The model's output distribution over the full vocabulary is then restricted to just two words, positive and negative. Every other token is ignored.

The prediction is whichever of the two the model assigns higher probability. Nothing is trained; the label is read out of the language model's own next-token distribution.

concepts.name: RACE Zero-Shot Heuristic
concepts.summary: Condition the generative model on the document and question, then pick the answer with the highest average token log-probability.
concepts.explanation:
For RACE the heuristic uses the multiple-choice structure directly.

The document and the question are fed in as context. Each candidate answer is then scored by the average token log-probability the model assigns it, conditioned on that context.

The prediction is the candidate scoring highest.

In effect the question becomes: which of these continuations does the language model find least surprising after reading the passage? Averaging rather than summing keeps answers of different lengths comparable.

concepts.name: DPRD Winograd-Schema Zero-Shot Heuristic
concepts.summary: Substitute each possible referent for the definite pronoun and choose the resolution under which the rest of the sentence scores higher.
concepts.explanation:
A Winograd-schema item is a sentence with an ambiguous definite pronoun whose correct referent turns on [[world-knowledge]] rather than grammar.

The heuristic makes the ambiguity explicit. The pronoun is replaced by each of the two possible referents in turn, producing two full sentences with nothing left to resolve.

The model then scores the rest of the sequence after the substitution, by average token log-probability, and the higher-scoring version wins.

The idea is that the wrong substitution makes the continuation less coherent, and a good language model registers that as lower probability.

This is the only one of the four heuristics that edits the input before scoring it.

citedFrom.refText: A. Rahman and V. Ng. Resolving complex cases of definite pronouns: the winograd schema challenge. EMNLP-CoNLL, 2012.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The DPRD dataset and the definite-pronoun-resolution format the heuristic operates on are defined there.

concepts.name: Structured Attentional Memory and Inductive Bias
concepts.summary: The paper's hypothesis that the transformer's attention gives it a more structured memory than an LSTM, which helps transfer.
concepts.explanation:
An LSTM compresses everything it has read into a fixed-size recurrent state, so information from far back competes for the same vector.

Attention keeps every earlier position addressable and retrieves from them on demand. The paper calls this a more structured attentional memory and hypothesizes that it assists in transfer compared with LSTMs.

The evidence offered is indirect. The LSTM shows higher variance in zero-shot performance across pre-training, while the transformer's heuristic scores are stable and rise steadily.

The paper's own wording is suggesting rather than showing. Stability differences on hand-designed heuristics are thin support for a claim about architectural bias, and the paper does not push it further.

concepts.name: Ablation Studies
concepts.summary: Three controlled removals reported in Table 5: dropping the auxiliary LM objective, replacing the transformer with an LSTM, and skipping pre-training entirely.
concepts.explanation:
The results tables show that the full system wins. The ablations ask which of its parts are doing the work.

Each removes one piece and holds the rest fixed. First the [[auxiliary-lm-objective|auxiliary language modelling objective]] is switched off during fine-tuning. Second the transformer is replaced by a single-layer 2048-unit LSTM in the same framework. Third the transformer is trained directly on the supervised tasks with no pre-training at all.

The sizes of the three effects are not equal, and that ordering is the finding.

Removing pre-training costs 14.8%, swapping the architecture costs 5.6 average score points, and the auxiliary objective helps only on some datasets.

So the ablations put pre-training first, the architecture second, and the auxiliary objective a distant and dataset-dependent third.

concepts.name: Ablation: No Auxiliary LM Objective
concepts.summary: Fine-tuning without the language modelling loss helps on some datasets and hurts on others, with larger datasets benefiting from keeping it.
concepts.explanation:
This ablation sets the auxiliary term to zero during fine-tuning, so only the supervised loss is optimized.

The result is not uniform. The paper reports that the auxiliary objective helps on the NLI tasks and on [[qqp]], and that the overall trend suggests larger datasets benefit from it while smaller ones do not.

One reading is that the extra objective acts as a regularizer whose value depends on how much supervised signal there is. With plenty of labelled data the extra pull is affordable and useful; with little, it competes with the task.

The paper labels this a trend rather than a rule, and does not test the size explanation directly.

concepts.name: Ablation: LSTM Instead of Transformer
concepts.summary: Replacing the transformer with a single-layer 2048-unit LSTM in the same framework costs 5.6 average score points.
concepts.explanation:
This ablation keeps the framework — the same pre-training, the same input transformations, the same fine-tuning procedure — and changes only the architecture.

The substitute is a single-layer LSTM with 2048 units. The paper reports a 5.6 average score drop relative to the transformer.

One exception is recorded: [[mrpc]] is the only dataset where the LSTM comes out ahead.

This is the ablation that isolates architecture from method, and it is the quantitative counterpart to the inductive-bias hypothesis in the zero-shot analysis. The paper reports the drop without attributing it to any particular property of the LSTM.

concepts.name: Ablation: No Pre-Training
concepts.summary: Training the same transformer directly on the supervised tasks, with no pre-training, costs 14.8% across the board.
concepts.explanation:
Here the architecture is unchanged and the [[generative-pretraining|generative pre-training]] stage is deleted. The transformer is trained on each supervised target task from scratch.

The paper reports that the lack of pre-training hurts performance across all the tasks, producing a 14.8% decrease compared with the full model.

Two details give this weight. The drop is uniform — across all the tasks, not concentrated in the small datasets where one would most expect it.

And it is roughly three times the cost of swapping the architecture.

This is the ablation that carries the paper's central claim. Whatever the transformer contributes, the unsupervised pre-training stage contributes more.
